passage: Two days before the college fest, a power cut hit the whole of Margao, and Maria, twenty-one and newly the council secretary, had forty posters still unprinted. She sent Simran and two first-years across town, in the rain, to a print shop with a generator, and told them to be back in an hour. When Simran messaged that the shop had a queue, Maria replied, "Figure it out, that's the job." Meanwhile she took the council's only umbrella and the office's spare key to charge her laptop in the principal's lounge, "just this once." At nine, Simran came back soaked and quiet. Maria barely looked up. "Why so late?" Later, on the bus home, Maria told her roommate she hadn't changed at all since first year. She honestly believed it.

qa.q: Where did Maria go to charge her laptop?
qa.a: Maria took the office's spare key to charge her laptop in the principal's lounge.

qa.q: Why doesn't Maria notice any change in herself?
qa.a: Maria feels confident she hasn't changed since first year; focused on her own deadline, she no longer sees how Simran and the juniors feel.

qa.q: What could Maria have chosen when Simran messaged about the queue?
qa.a: Maria could have asked how they were managing in the rain, shared the umbrella or moved the deadline, instead of replying "Figure it out, that's the job."

qa.q: How might Simran see Maria when coming back soaked and quiet?
qa.a: Simran might feel unseen and used, since Maria stayed dry, bent the rules for herself and only asked "Why so late?"

grounding: Shows a student leader under fest pressure growing careless of juniors' feelings and bending rules for herself while believing she is unchanged.

passage: Three months into his internship at a design studio in Salt Lake, Anirban was asked to guide the two newest interns. He was pleased; he had always hated how the seniors ignored him. Within weeks, though, he was sending Jeevan back to redo slides at 7 p.m. while he left at six, "because I've done my hours." He started using the good corner desk everyone was supposed to share, and signed his own name at the bottom of a poster Jeevan had drawn most of. When Jeevan mentioned missing the last metro twice, Anirban said, "Welcome to the real world," and went back to his phone. On Friday he told his mother he was still the same easygoing Anirban from college. He didn't notice that she didn't answer.

qa.q: What did Anirban say when Jeevan mentioned missing the last metro?
qa.a: Anirban said, "Welcome to the real world," and went back to his phone.

qa.q: Why does Anirban believe nothing has changed?
qa.a: Anirban feels comfortable still seeing himself as the easygoing person from college, and is too wrapped up in his own hours to notice how Jeevan is affected.

qa.q: Which moment could have been a turning point for Anirban, and what could he do?
qa.a: When his mother didn't answer, Anirban could have asked why and looked honestly at the late slides, the corner desk and the poster credit.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban remembered how the seniors ignored him?
qa.a: Anirban might treat Jeevan the way he once wished to be treated: leaving on time, sharing the desk and giving credit for the poster.

grounding: Illustrates an intern with a little authority growing less attentive to a junior and taking perks, while believing he is the same person.

passage:
"Manoj bhaiya, you've been on the phone for an hour," Siddharth said, dropping onto the sofa.
"Mess committee stuff. The juniors messed up the Diwali menu." Manoj covered the phone, then spoke into it. "No, Aakash, I don't care if your exam is tomorrow. Redo the list tonight."
"He has an exam tomorrow?"
"Everyone has exams. I had exams too."
"You also got extra paneer from the mess every night last month. You told me."
"Secretary perk. Not a big deal."
"Last year you fought the old secretary for doing exactly that."
Manoj frowned. "That was different. He was arrogant."
"Bhaiya, you just told a junior you don't care."
"I said it nicely." Manoj looked down at his phone. "Didn't I?"
"You sounded like the old secretary."
"I'm the same person, Siddharth."
Siddharth shrugged and reached for the remote. "Okay. Just saying."

qa.q: What did Manoj say the juniors messed up?
qa.a: Manoj said the juniors messed up the Diwali menu.

qa.q: What does Manoj's "Didn't I?" suggest he is starting to feel?
qa.a: It suggests a flicker of doubt: for a moment Manoj wonders whether he really sounded harsh, though he still insists he's the same person 🤔

qa.q: What could Manoj do after that moment of doubt?
qa.a: Manoj could call Aakash back, let the list wait until after the exam, and give up the extra paneer.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the change in Manoj?
qa.a: Siddharth sees Manoj turning into the arrogant old secretary he once fought, taking perks and brushing off a junior's exam.

grounding: Shows a student mess secretary at home for Diwali dismissing a junior and taking perks, sure he has not changed while his brother notices.

passage: I'm Harish. In my third year of college I was made senior under-officer at the NCC camp. It was the proudest day of my life, and I'm only now seeing what came after. I stopped noticing the juniors' faces. When Ojas, a first-year, said, "Sir, my blisters are bleeding, can I skip one drill?" I told him, "Blisters build character," and moved on. The same week I skipped the cold dawn run myself, twice, telling myself I had admin work. I took the only bunk near the heater. If you had asked me then, I would have sworn I was the same easygoing Harish who used to share my blanket on the train. It was Ojas limping at the passing-out parade that finally made me see it. Too late for his feet.

qa.q: Why did Ojas ask to skip one drill?
qa.a: Because his blisters were bleeding.

qa.q: How did Harish see himself during the camp, and what shows the gap?
qa.a: He believed he was still the same easygoing person, yet he dismissed Ojas's blisters and bent the rules for himself by skipping the dawn run and taking the bunk near the heater.

qa.q: What could Harish have done differently when Ojas asked to skip the drill?
qa.a: He could have looked at the blisters, let Ojas rest or see the camp medic, and followed the same rules he set for others.

qa.q: What was the camp like for Ojas under Harish?
qa.a: Ojas felt unheard and in pain, having to keep drilling with bleeding feet while his senior skipped runs himself.

grounding: A student given rank at camp becomes less attentive to a junior's pain and bends rules for himself, without noticing the change.

passage:
Lab manager's note, 18 July. Written by Mrs Nair.

Yogesh, twenty-one, was made lead of our summer intern batch three weeks ago. He's capable, and I chose him for his friendliness. Since then I've seen some changes. He gave himself the only fast computer and left early two Fridays while the others stayed to finish sample logs. When Dhruv, the youngest intern, asked for help with a calibration he had never done, Yogesh said, "Read the manual, I learned it alone," and put his headphones back on. Dhruv redid the calibration three times and missed his train.

When I raised this, Yogesh looked genuinely surprised. "Ma'am, I'm the same as always. I just have more responsibility now." I believe he means it.

My next step: a short weekly meeting where each intern, Dhruv included, tells me one thing that helped and one that didn't, with Yogesh present.

qa.q: What did Yogesh give himself after becoming lead?
qa.a: He gave himself the only fast computer.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh look surprised when Mrs Nair raised the problem?
qa.a: He genuinely believed he was the same as always and had not noticed he was bending rules and ignoring juniors.

qa.q: Why could the weekly meeting help Yogesh?
qa.a: Hearing what did and didn't help from the interns themselves would show him how juniors feel, which his new role has made him stop noticing.

qa.q: How did Yogesh's change affect Dhruv?
qa.a: Dhruv was left to struggle alone with a calibration he had never done, redid it three times and missed his train.

grounding: A new intern lead grows less attentive to juniors and bends rules for himself, while sincerely believing he has not changed.

passage: Zubin, twenty, had been elected student council president in September. By November he walked straight to the front of the canteen queue because he had "a meeting." He booked the seminar hall for council events without asking the drama club, who'd reserved it first. When Gargi, a first-year, came to his office in tears because her scholarship form had been lost by the council, he glanced at his phone. "I'll look into it." He didn't. That evening, Gargi's friend told Zubin, "She's been waiting three days." Zubin frowned. "I'm busy with the fest. She can wait a bit." He genuinely believed he was the same Zubin who used to sit on the steps with first-years. He hadn't noticed that he no longer asked anyone how they were.

qa.q: How long had Gargi been waiting?
qa.a: She's been waiting three days.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she came to Zubin's office?
qa.a: Gargi was anxious and upset, in tears because her scholarship form had been lost.

qa.q: What could Zubin do to catch this drift early?
qa.a: He could ask a trusted friend how he comes across, and follow up personally on juniors' problems like Gargi's.

qa.q: How might the drama club see Zubin's hall booking?
qa.a: The drama club likely felt ignored and resentful, since they had reserved the hall first.

grounding: A student leader becomes less attentive to how juniors feel and bends rules for himself, without noticing he has changed.

passage:
"Mehak, can I leave at six today? My mother's got a hospital appointment."
Mehak didn't look up from her laptop. "Divyansh, we're behind on the deck. Everyone stays."
"But you left at four yesterday."
"That was for a client dinner. Different."
"Okay." Divyansh paused. "Also, the research I did for slide eight. You presented it as yours in the meeting."
"It's team work. I'm the lead intern. That's how it works."
"Last month you said credit should always go to whoever did it."
Mehak finally looked up, annoyed. "Last month I wasn't responsible for the whole team."
Divyansh stood there, then went back to his desk. Mehak returned to her slides, a little irritated. She didn't think anything had changed. She was just busier now. She didn't notice that she hadn't asked about his mother.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh want to leave at six?
qa.a: His mother had a hospital appointment.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when Divyansh raised slide eight?
qa.a: Mehak felt annoyed and defensive, sure her new role justified what she did.

qa.q: What could Mehak do if she wanted to stay the same person as a lead?
qa.a: She could apply the same rules to herself, credit Divyansh for his research, and ask how juniors are doing, not just what they owe.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel walking back to his desk?
qa.a: Divyansh likely felt hurt and unheard, since Mehak ignored both his mother's appointment and his work.

grounding: A lead intern with some authority stops noticing juniors' feelings and bends rules for herself, while believing she hasn't changed.

passage: When I became hostel secretary in second year, I honestly thought I was the same person. I'm Disha. But looking back, I can see the slide. I stopped queueing for the washing machine; I had "duties." I let my friends stay past curfew and wrote up juniors who did the same. When Dilnaz, a first-year, came to me because her roommate's music kept her awake before exams, I told her to "adjust." I remember thinking she was being dramatic. Later I found out she'd been crying most nights. The worst part was that I didn't notice any of it at the time. I just felt busy and important. It was only when my old friend said, "You used to ask people how they were," that I felt the floor tilt.

qa.q: What did Disha tell Dilnaz to do?
qa.a: Disha told her to "adjust."

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the old friend spoke up?
qa.a: Disha felt shaken and ashamed, as if the floor tilted, realising how much had changed.

qa.q: What could have kept Disha from drifting?
qa.a: Keeping the same rules for Disha and friends as for juniors, and regularly asking juniors how they were, might have kept her empathy.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have experienced being told to adjust?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably felt dismissed and alone, which is why she was crying most nights.

grounding: A former hostel secretary looks back on how authority made the secretary less attentive to juniors and quicker to bend rules, without noticing at the time.

passage:
Supervisor's note, summer internship, week 6
In week 2, I put Madhav in charge of two first-year trainees, Charu and another student. He did well at first: checked in, explained tasks.
Since week 4 I've noticed changes. He now leaves early on Fridays, "because leads can." He didn't notice when Charu stayed till eight fixing his slides. When she asked for help with a spreadsheet, he said, "Figure it out, that's how I learned."
Yesterday I asked him how his team was doing. "Great," he said. "I'm the same as I was, just busier."
Next week I'll ask Charu and the other trainee to fill in a short anonymous feedback form, and I'll go through it with Madhav.

qa.q: When did the supervisor put Madhav in charge of the trainees?
qa.a: Madhav was put in charge in week 2.

qa.q: What does Madhav's answer "I'm the same as I was" suggest?
qa.a: He feels confident and a bit self-satisfied, not noticing how he has changed toward his juniors.

qa.q: Why could the feedback form help?
qa.a: It lets Charu and the other trainee say how they feel without fear, so Madhav can see what he isn't noticing.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu when Madhav tells her to figure it out?
qa.a: Charu feels unsupported and a little hurt, having stayed till eight fixing his slides.

grounding: Shows an intern given authority becoming less attentive to juniors and bending rules for himself, while believing he has not changed.

passage:
Friday night
Long day. As council president I had to sort out the fest budget again. I'm Vasudha, and honestly I'm the only one who takes this seriously.
Nitin from first year came to my desk with a question about volunteer passes. I told him to email. He looked a bit lost, but I really didn't have time.
I also took the council room for my group study. Technically it's only for meetings, but I've earned it.
At dinner, my old roommate said I've "changed." I haven't. I'm exactly the same person. I'm just busier and people expect more from me now.
Anyway, I need sleep. Tomorrow: fest meeting at 9.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha take the group study?
qa.a: Vasudha took the council room for group study.

qa.q: How does Vasudha seem to feel about the roommate's comment?
qa.a: Vasudha feels defensive and a bit irritated, insisting nothing has changed.

qa.q: What small step could help Vasudha notice what the roommate sees?
qa.a: Vasudha could ask juniors like Nitin how things feel to them, and follow the same room rules as everyone else.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nitin to be told to email?
qa.a: Nitin may feel dismissed and unsure, having come in person with a simple question.

grounding: Shows a student leader less attentive to a junior's feelings and bending a rule for their own benefit, while believing nothing has changed.

passage: In the small town of Pala, Joseph was made team leader of the NGO's summer survey. The month before, as a volunteer, he had carried water to the others and noticed who was tired. Now he had a clipboard and a motorbike. He rode ahead while the volunteers walked in the heat. He gave himself the shaded houses near the church. When Rajni, a volunteer, asked for an hour off for her mother's hospital visit, he said, 'Targets first,' without looking up. That same week he took Friday afternoon off to watch a football match. At night, writing his report, he thought: I'm the same Joseph. I'm just busier.

qa.q: What did Joseph do in the month before, as a volunteer?
qa.a: He carried water to the others and noticed who was tired.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about himself while writing his report?
qa.a: Joseph feels comfortable and unbothered, sure he is still the same, just busier.

qa.q: What could help Joseph notice the change?
qa.a: Walking with the volunteers again, or asking Rajni and others for honest feedback on how he leads.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel after hearing 'Targets first'?
qa.a: Rajni probably felt hurt and dismissed, especially when she saw Joseph take Friday off for football.

grounding: A young team leader in a small town grows less attentive to volunteers and bends rules for himself without noticing.

passage: Tuan had been elected head of the student union at his Hanoi university in September. By November the first-years noticed he had changed. He used to eat with them in the canteen; now he ate in the union office with the door shut. When Hana, a first-year, came to complain that the new dorm curfew was unfair to students with late lab classes, he checked his phone while she talked and said, 'Send an email.' She did. It sat unread for three weeks. Meanwhile he gave himself a late-night pass 'for union business' and parked in the staff lot. When an old friend teased him about the parking, Tuan laughed. 'I'm exactly the same person. I just have more responsibility.'

qa.q: Where does Tuan eat now?
qa.a: In the union office with the door shut.

qa.q: How does Tuan feel when teased about the parking?
qa.a: Tuan feels unbothered and a bit amused, sure he is exactly the same person.

qa.q: What could Tuan do to stay in touch with first-years?
qa.a: Eat in the canteen again, answer complaints like Hana's promptly, and apply the curfew to himself too.

qa.q: How might Hana feel when her email sits unread?
qa.a: Hana likely feels ignored and frustrated, as if her concern didn't matter to someone students voted for.

grounding: A student leader abroad stops attending to juniors' feelings and bends rules for himself while believing he hasn't changed.

passage: Three months into her internship at the research lab, Trisha was put in charge of the two undergraduate helpers, and something in her shifted. She stopped saying please. She sent Pradeep, a second-year, to wash glassware during the one talk he had asked to attend. When he mentioned it, she said, 'Everyone starts at the sink,' though she had never washed a beaker in her life. She began leaving at five while the helpers stayed till seven. In the lab meeting she took credit for their data cleaning without thinking. If anyone had asked, she would have said she was still the friendly Trisha from the canteen. Pradeep, eating alone by the sink window, no longer thought so.

qa.q: Where did Trisha send Pradeep during the talk?
qa.a: To wash glassware.

qa.q: What does Trisha feel about herself during these months?
qa.a: Trisha feels unchanged and comfortable, believing she is still the friendly Trisha from the canteen.

qa.q: What small changes could bring back Trisha's care for the helpers?
qa.a: Letting Pradeep attend talks, sharing credit for their work and keeping the same hours as the helpers.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel about the new Trisha?
qa.a: Pradeep feels hurt and resentful, eating alone and no longer seeing her as friendly.

grounding: A young intern given a little authority grows less attentive to juniors and bends rules for herself without noticing.

passage:
Dear Parul,
Happy Navratri! Our hostel did garba in the courtyard, and as general secretary I got to open it. Very filmy, I know.
Honestly, being GS is exhausting. The first-years keep coming to my room about the mess food and the broken geysers. I told them to put it in writing and stop whining; we all survived first year. One of them started crying in the corridor, which, really, was a bit much.
Best perk: committee members can come back after the 10 pm curfew "for meetings". I've used it three times this week, twice just for chai at the bus stand. The warden never checks.
Don't worry, Parul, I'm still the same Salma who cried at our school farewell. Power hasn't gone to my head, ha!
Write soon,
Salma

qa.q: How many times did Salma use the late-return perk this week?
qa.a: Three times, twice just for chai at the bus stand.

qa.q: How does Salma seem to feel about the first-years' complaints?
qa.a: Salma seems irritated and dismissive, calling the crying a bit much, without noticing how upset the juniors are.

qa.q: What could Salma do if Parul points out the change?
qa.a: Salma could go back and hear the first-years' mess and geyser complaints properly, and stop using the curfew exception for chai.

qa.q: How might the first-year who cried in the corridor see Salma?
qa.a: That student probably sees a cold senior who brushes off real problems, not the kind person Salma believes is still there.

grounding: A student leader stops noticing how juniors feel and bends the curfew rule for personal chai, while believing nothing has changed.
